proposals.observation: The Daily Blog Post workflow failed at 06:50 on 2 July. The content queue shows only 1 post queued against 47 published, meaning the pipeline that writes and queues new posts has stalled. With zero quiz sessions in 48 hours, organic discovery depends entirely on fresh blog content indexed by search. A broken publishing workflow compounds every other acquisition problem: no new posts, no long-tail traffic, no new names entering the automations that are currently performing well.
proposals.proposal: Inspect the failed Daily Blog Post workflow run, find the first error line in the logs, and fix it. The most common causes for this workflow class are: expired API key in GitHub Actions secrets, a changed model name in the LLM call, or a malformed frontmatter template that fails schema validation against src/content.config.ts. Because .github/workflows/* is a blocked path, the fix must go into whatever non-workflow file the workflow calls — most likely a script file or a prompt template. Pull the exact error from the Actions log before touching anything. Ship only the minimum change that clears the failure.

proposals.observation: The Funnel-Hack Digest workflow also failed, at 11:20 on the same day. Two workflow failures on the same calendar day points to a shared dependency: a secrets rotation, a package version bump, or an upstream API change that hit both jobs. Fixing the blog workflow first will surface whether the root cause is shared. If the Funnel-Hack Digest fails for a different reason, it needs its own fix. This digest presumably feeds Joel's content strategy and competitor awareness; a silent failure means stale intelligence accumulates without anyone noticing.
proposals.proposal: After resolving Proposal 1, open the Funnel-Hack Digest failure log and compare the error to what was found in the blog workflow. If the root cause is identical (same secret, same dependency), the fix is already shipped and a manual re-run of the digest workflow confirms it. If the error differs, identify the specific failing step — likely a scrape target returning a changed HTML structure, or a summarisation prompt hitting a token or rate limit — and patch the calling script or prompt file accordingly. Document the fix in a commit message that names the exact error so future Fred runs can spot the pattern.

proposals.impact: converts highest-open automation into booked calls
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has the highest open rate of the three active sequences: 66.67% across 12 sends. Money Avoidance sits at 52.63% and Money Worship at 37.5%. High open rate on a short sequence means the subject line and sender trust are working, but there is no data showing whether those opens convert to discovery calls or any other downstream action. With quiz sessions at zero, these automations are the only warm touchpoints Joel has right now. The Vigilance sequence is the place to add or sharpen a call-to-action while attention is highest.
proposals.proposal: Add one plain-text CTA paragraph to the final email in the Money Vigilance sequence. The paragraph should name what vigilance costs in practice (the thing the reader already knows but has not said aloud) and offer a single next step: a 45-minute call. No button, no image, no urgency device. The copy below is written to pass the Sultanic test — it references the specific texture of vigilance behaviour rather than describing the concept from outside.
proposals.new_text:
If you recognise yourself in this sequence, you already know the specific feeling I mean. The spreadsheet you check before a social plan. The pause before you agree to anything that costs money, even when the cost is genuinely fine. The background hum that does not stop when the balance is healthy.

That quiet monitoring is not a flaw. It kept you careful when careful mattered. The question worth sitting with now is whether it is still working for you, or whether it has started working against you.

If you want to think it through with someone who will not tell you to spend more freely or stress less about money, you can book a 45-minute call with me here: [BOOKING_LINK]

Joel Donoghue, MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner
